column2: Tapini, Tapini, Dhumra, Marichi, Jvalini, Ruchi, Sushumna, Bhogada, Vishva, Bodhini, Dharini and Kshama.
In that vessel is the supreme nectar, cause of supreme bliss, rich with the essences of all herbs and joined with delightful fragrance,
ever perfumed with blue lotuses and white water-lilies, unwithered and very fragrant, delightful, cool, light and pure,
noble with hundreds of moving waves, fit for the worship of Lalita, ever resounding, it shines as the means of worship.
That offering-water is called nectar, made of the digits of the moon; in it are small boats made of gems, where the lovely digits of the moon, in fresh youth, play.
Amrita, Manada, Pusha, Tushti, Pushti, Rati, Dhriti, Shashini, Chandrika, Kanti, Jyotsna, Shri, Priti, Angada,
Purna and Purnamrita — these are the digits of the nectar-rayed moon, full of fresh youth, their faces ever smiling.
Pushti, Riddhi, Sthiti, Medha, Kanti, Lakshmi, Dyuti, Dhriti, Jara and Siddhi — these are declared the digits of Brahma, who play there.
Sthiti, Palini, Shanti, Ishvari, Rati, Kamika, Varada, Ahladini, Priti and Dirgha — these are the digits of Hari.
Tikshna, Raudri, Bhaya, Nidra, Tandra, Kshut, Krodhini, Trapa, Utkari and Mrityu — these digits of Rudra dwell there.
The digits of Ishvara are yellow, white, ruddy and pale — four are declared. Now the digits of Shankara:
Nivritti, Pratishtha, Vidya, Shanti, Indira, Dipika, Rechika, Mochika,
Para, Sukshma, O enemy of the Vindhya, Sukshmamrita, Jnanamrita, Vyadhini, Vyapini and Vyomarupika — these sixteen are declared; these Shaktis play there.
Mounted on Rudra's boats, moving restlessly here and there, thousands of sciences play there in the form of Shaktis.
They were devised by the Supreme One for the purification of the offering-water; drinking that nectar of the offering, the Shaktis are ever intoxicated.
Dwelling in the great lotus forest and stationed in the great chakra, again and again, ever fresh and ever fragrant,
with thousands of jewelled pots and crores of golden jars they constantly fill up that great nectar of the offering,
and the attendant Shaktis of those dwelling in the house of the wish-granting gem, exultant, offer it to the Shaktis beginning with Anima.
Thus the arrangement of the offering in the eastern part of the great lotus-forest enclosure has been told; next, other things there are described.
Full of fresh beauty, their lotus faces smiling, blazing wish-granting gems in their hands, ever sixteen years old, of exceedingly noble nature, they play, overcome with intoxication.
Above that enclosure of Anima and the rest is a very charming platform, twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide,
very beautiful with rows of steps in the four directions; it is the seat of Brahmi and the others. Hear of the goddesses stationed there:
Brahmi, Maheshvari, Kaumari, Vaishnavi, Varahi, Mahendri, Chamunda the seventh, and Mahalakshmi the eighth — these have made their abodes there,
rich in various weapons, with retinues of various Shaktis, their dwellings arranged sunwise beginning from the east.
Then above that enclosure of Brahmi and the rest, O pot-born one, twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide, is the enclosure of the Mudras, threefold; there the Mudras have their abodes:
Sankshobha, Dravana, Akarsha, Vashya, Unmada, Mahankusha, Khechari, Bija, Yoni, and Trikhanda the tenth.
These Mudras are established beginning from the east, exceedingly beautiful in form, overwhelmed with fresh youth,
filling the inner house with lovely radiance; they serve Lalita, the supreme Queen, O tiger among sages.
These three enclosures form the chakra that bewitches the three worlds; the Shaktis in it are declared by the name Prakata.
Their presiding deity is Tripura, leader of the chakra; the Mudra that guards that chakra is Sankshobhana.
Then above the Mudra enclosure is declared the enclosure of the eternal digits, twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide, with mountain-like steps rising one above another.
In that enclosure of eternal digits, the Shaktis beginning with Kamakarshanika, consisting of the sixteen digits of the moon, are stationed all around,
delighting the circle of directions with very cool streams of nectar. Learn their names from me, O pot-born one:
Kamakarshinika Nitya, Buddhyakarshanika, Rasakarshanika Nitya, Gandhakarshanika Kala,
Chittakarshanika Nitya, Dhairyakarshanika Kala, Smrityakarshanika Nitya, Namakarshanika Kala,
Bijakarshanika Nitya, Arthakarshanika Kala, another Amritakarshani, and Sharirakarshani Kala.
These are the Gupta Yoginis; Tripureshi is the Chakrini; the presiding deity of the chakra is called Sarvashapurika.
The guardian in this chakra is the Mudra named Dravinika. Above the enclosure of eternal digits is an exceedingly beautiful seat,
twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide, with steps as before, called Sarvasankshobhana.
There eight fierce Shaktis, their eyes red with intoxication, intoxicated with fresh youth, serve the supreme Queen:
Kusuma, Mekhala, Madana, Madanatura, Rekha, Vegini, Ankusha and Malini — these eight Shaktis.
Their retinue is crores of Shaktis beginning with Ananga. This chakra is Sarvasankshobha; its presiding deity
should be known as Sundari, also named Guptatara; the Mudra that guards that chakra is remembered as Akarshanika.
Above the enclosure of the Ananga Shaktis, O pot-born one, twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide, is the enclosure of Sankshobhini and the rest, which grants all good fortune.
The fierce Shaktis led by Sarvasankshobhini dwell there, fourteen of them; hear their names from me:
the Shakti Sarvasankshobhini, Sarvavidravini, the Shakti Sarvakarshanika, Sarvahladanika,
the Shakti Sarvasammohini, the Shakti Sarvastambhana, the Shakti Sarvajrimbhinika and Sarvavashankari,
the Shakti Sarvaranjana, the Shakti Sarvonmadini, the Shakti Sarvarthasadhika, Sarvasampattipurini,
the Shakti Sarvamantramayi and Sarvadvandvakshayankari. These are called the Sampradayas, dwelling in the city of the Chakrini.
The Mudras called Sarvavashya are regarded as the protectors in that chakra; crores of Shaktis there are their servants.
Above the enclosure of Sankshobhini and the rest, O pot-born one, twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide, is said to be the seat and mansion of Sarvasiddhi and the others:
Sarvasiddhiprada, Sarvasampatprada, the goddess Sarvapriyankari, Sarvamangalakarini,
the goddess Sarvakamaprada, Sarvaduhkhavimochani, Sarvamrityuprashamini, Sarvavighnanivarini,
the goddess Sarvangasundari and Sarvasaubhagyadayini — these goddesses are remembered by name as the Kalotkirna Yoginis.
The Chakrini should be known as Shri, and the chakra as Sarvarthasadhaka; the Sarvonmadana Mudras are the guardians of the chakra.
Above the enclosure of Sarvasiddhi and the rest, O pot-born one, twenty cubits high and four nalvas wide,
is the enclosure called Sarvajna and the rest, remembered as Sarvarakshakara — a great divine chakra; those beginning with Sarvajna are declared:
Sarvajna, Sarvashakti, Sarvaishvaryapradayini, the goddess Sarvajnanamayi, Sarvavyadhivinashini,
Sarvadharasvarupa, Sarvapapahari, the goddess Sarvanandamayi, Sarvarakshasvarupini,
and Sarvepsitaprada — these are the Nirgarbha lords of Yoginis.

Malini is declared the Chakrini, and the Mudra is Sarvamahankusha. Thus some of the chakras in the house of the wish-granting gem, up to the enclosure of Sarvajna and the rest, have been told; hear of others too, O sage.
Hriddevi, Shirodevi, Shikhadevi, Varmadevi, Drishtidevi and Shastradevi — six are named.
They are exceedingly close to the fair-browed consort of Kameshvara, their limbs full of fresh beauty, attentive and bearing weapons.
Moving around the dot-seat with proud forms, executing Lalita's commands, they stand at the seat of the self-controlled ones.
Then above the enclosure of the limb-goddesses is the circular great seat of Bindu and Nada, ten cubits high,
eight nalvas wide, like the rising sun. This should be known as the Bindu-pitha; it is also called the Shri-pitha,
and should be known as the Mahapitha; it is also called the Vidya-pitha and the Ananda-pitha, bearing the form of the fifty seats.
There the great jewelled couch of Goddess Shri Lalita, made of the five Brahmans, the root of the three worlds, keeps watch.
The four legs of that couch are declared to be ten cubits high and three cubits thick,
having taken the forms of Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesha and Ishvara, and having attained the state of Shakti through constant yoga of meditation on the Goddess.
One leg, like the hibiscus flower, should be known as consisting of Brahma, occupying the south-eastern direction.
The fourth leg of the couch, with the lustre of the karnikara's essence, should be known as consisting of Ishvara, occupying the north-eastern direction.
All of these are armed and adorned with every ornament, in the form of pillars above and below and in the form of persons in the middle,
their eyes closed in meditation on the Goddess and their limbs motionless through that meditation. Above them the board of the couch is Sadashiva,
with the hue of a blooming pomegranate, four nalvas wide and six nalvas long, of ever-shining form.
From the beginning of the enclosure of the limb-goddesses up to the board of the couch, the steps, made of wish-granting gems and embodying the principles, O ascetic,
shine with thirty-six stages. We name the steps in the order of ascent:
earth, water, fire, air, space, smell, taste, form, touch, sound, the organs of generation and excretion, the feet,
hands, speech, nose, tongue, skin, eye and ear, egoity, intellect, mind, Prakriti and Purusha,
Niyati, Kala and Raga, Kala and Vidya with Maya, Shuddhavidya, Ishvara, Sadashiva, Shakti and Shiva.
These thirty-six are declared the rows of steps of the principles; the row of steps faces the eastern direction of the couch.
Then above the couch is a bed with a swan-down mattress, a cubit high and four nalvas wide,
adorned with a pair of pillows at the feet and head, and beautiful with sixty-four cushions of rosy hue.
Above that is a coverlet of safflower-coloured cloth, pure and soft, with the lustre of rubies.
Dwelling on it, facing east, full of compassion, beautiful in amorous attire, ever sixteen years old,
like the orb of the rising sun, four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with necklace, armlets, crown and bracelets,
his cheeks filled with the moonlight of a lovely smile, the Lord, the primal god, Kameshvara Shiva, keeps watch.
Seated on his lap, rosy as the young sun, ever sixteen years old, proud of fresh youth,
with the lustre of unpolished rubies, her nails like sandal-lotuses, needing no lac-dye, her feet flowing with natural redness,
enchanting with sweetly tinkling anklets and slipping bracelets, her shanks crushing the pride of the bodiless one's fine quiver,
beautiful with thighs like an elephant's trunk and the lustre of plantain stems, her ample hips adorned with fine, soft-to-touch red silk, radiant in the expanse of her loins,
with a knot at mid-thigh, resplendent with a jewelled girdle, a river whose waves are the three folds and whose great whirlpool is her deep navel,
covered with hundreds of strings of pearls swinging on the buds of her breasts, her waist bending under the weight of very full breasts,
her four arms soft as garlands of shirisha flowers,
adorned with rows of armlets and bracelets, with rings on her fingers; her lovely conch-like neck bearing her husband's touch,
her chin round like a mirror, her lips rosy; with pure rows of bright teeth, radiant like forms of knowledge, with the beauty of jasmine buds, she displays moonlight,
radiant with various ornaments set with large pearls, her eyes long, like the inner petals of the ketaka,
her forehead lovely as the half-moon with locks well arranged, her ears adorned with ruby earrings,
her betel ever fragrant with fresh camphor and musk, her face sweet like the orb of the bright autumn moon,
wearing a lovely crown made of the essence of wish-granting gems, resplendent with a forehead-eye like a gleaming tilaka jewel,
her mass of hair dense as deep darkness, radiant with a line of vermilion placed in the parting of her hair,
crowned with a gleaming crescent moon, her eyes rolling with intoxication, rich in all amorous attire and adorned with every ornament,
mother of all the worlds, ever increasing bliss, the source of Brahma, Vishnu, Girisha, Isha and Sadashiva,
satisfying all with the stream of compassion rippling from the corners of her eyes — there shines that Blessed One, Lalitambika, destroyer of sin.
The worship of other deities is known to have the fruit of her worship; the fruit of her worship, they say, is her worship itself.
How then can I describe that Goddess Lalita? Not even a single part of her can be described in thousands of crores of years.
Being described, she is beyond speech; how can words reach her, from whom words turn back, unable to reach her along with the mind?
What use is saying much here? Hear this truth; I say it not from partiality, affection or delusion.
Let the branches of the wish-fulfilling tree be pens, O treasure of austerity, and let all the seven great oceans be inkpots;
let the earth, fifty crores wide, become the paper; let the time for writing be more than a parardha of years;
let all the worlds write, each with a crore of arms, and let all the speakers be equal to Brihaspati, O pot-born one —
even then not a thousandth part of the lustre of a single toe of that Goddess's lotus feet could be described. Indeed all effort to praise her virtues is fruitless.
Around the Bindu-pitha, in a square, hangs the curtain of Mahamaya, dark in hue.
Above the Goddess, forty cubits up, is fastened a canopy the colour of the cochineal insect, rare in the three worlds.
The array of ornaments there is exceedingly rare; my speech, as it set out to describe it, is stopped in my throat by shame.
She alone knows all of it, every virtue there; that beauty is beyond even the mind — by whom can it be described?
Thus Lalitambika, having appeared from the fire of consciousness to slay the great Daitya Bhanda, burned up all the Danavas.
Presiding over Shrinagara with its sixteen regions built by the divine artisans, she ever protects the world.
In this very manner there are other Shripuras too; there is no difference in arrangement, only in the names of the cities.
Those who tell the story of Shripura in order, beginning with the great garden of various trees, attain the supreme goal.
Those men who listen, ask and investigate, and those who keep it in a book, attain the supreme goal.
Those devotees who, following the plan of Shripura with its various places, have a great temple of the Goddess built entirely by artisans, attain the supreme goal.
His speech is sweet like the flood of the Mandakini; nothing in all the scriptures is unknown to him, O pot-born one.
He is able to establish and to refute all the systems of philosophy; he knows the whole truth and attains omniscience.
His heart is ever moist with compassion for all creatures; the three worlds cannot withstand the fire of his anger.
At the moment of seeing him, their skirt-knots loosening, their girdle-bands slipping, their earrings falling,
their forms adorned with pearls of sweat-drops, the corners of their eyes moving with intense longing,
the rows of jewelled bracelets slipping from their lotus hands, motionless with thighs stiff as pillars, their faces bowed with shame,
melting with love, adorned with bristling hair, as if transformed into another shape by the mind-born god,
as if blazing with masses of flames of unrestrained passion, as if gazed upon by showers of the fire of the bodiless one's arrows,
tormented by longing, wearied by the heat of their bodies, drenched with sweat and burning with shame,
abandoning family, caste, character, modesty and household, fear of the world, fear of kinsmen and fear of the next world,
the doe-eyed women beg for him in their hearts; whether in forest or city, in temple or monastery, wherever he stays, the doe-eyed ones run to him.
As a drop of water, struck hard, wanders on a lotus leaf, so the minds of fair-browed women wander at the sight of him.
He has the great fruit of melting even the most disciplined; the ranks of all the sciences serve him.
The woman of the three worlds, beautiful with breasts like the two orbs of moon and sun, falls in love with him at sight; what need to speak of other poor women, O ascetic?
In cities, streets, squares and forests, the holy proclamation of his fame is ever like the tree of heaven.
At the sight of him the net of sins of sinners perishes; his virtues alone will be proclaimed everywhere by the best of poets.
Those who meditate on the great Goddess with different colours, different weapons, and different mounts and ornaments obtain those respective perfections.
The first section of the mantra, radiant white as jasmine and the moon, blazing with flames in the chakra of day, should be meditated on at the root centre.
The second section of the mantra, like the cochineal insect, is to be contemplated in the chakra of day, its flame blazing up to the tip.
Then, in the hollow of the two-petalled lotus of the lotus of Bala and the others, the third section, which destroys sin, is to be contemplated.
For liberation, Ambika should be meditated on as white as moonlight; in the rite of subjugation she has the radiance of the red twilight;
for obtaining all wealth she is conceived as dark-limbed; blue for making others dumb; yellow in the rite of paralysis;
for poetic power she is clear in form, pure as crystal; for obtaining wealth Lalitambika is conceived as golden.
Those who meditate on the great mass of light, like a blazing ruby lamp, from the root centre to the aperture of Brahma, become accomplished in all perfections.
Thus, contemplating the Goddess in many ways through different meditations, O pot-born one, they attain great fortune. She is attained only by the good, never by the wicked.

She is meditated on within the self only by those who have practised intense austerity. One for whom this is not the last birth, or who is not himself Shankara, cannot obtain the knowledge of Lalita, the supreme Queen.
If this mantra comes to anyone's family, all the members of that family become liberated and satisfied, without doubt.
She is determined in all the scriptures to be more secret than the secret. The Vedas and all the scriptures praise Lalita, the Queen.
She alone is the Supreme Self; she alone is the highest goal; she alone is the great holy place; she alone is the great fruit.
The sages sing of her; Sanaka and the others meditate on her; the best of the gods, Brahma and the rest, worship her who grants the fivefold perfection.
She is not attained by those of evil conduct, the contemptible and crooked-minded, those outside divine grace, those of vain reasoning and vainly confused intellect,
the ruined, the ill-behaved, the defiled, those fallen from family, the harsh, the haters of philosophy, the sinful and revilers of good conduct,
the arrogant and insolent of speech, the hypocrites and the exceedingly proud; for such mortals, and even for gods, she is very hard to attain.
Her worthiness of worship even by the gods has been told, O pot-born one; she appeared from the fire of consciousness to slay Bhandasura.
The form of Mahatripurasundari, expanding in splendour, was named Kamakshi and Lalita, the Queen, by the Creator.
Because she delighted the mind of Sadashiva, who meditated on the supreme Lalitambika with supreme devotion, she is named Lalita.
All the deeds she performed have been told, and the whole method of worship according to the way stated in the scriptures. In another section I shall tell of her greatly wondrous play.
He had the wedding of that primal couple performed. The gods beginning with Indra, the Vasus, Rudras and other deities,
the sages led by Markandeya, the great sages led by Vasishtha, the lords of yogins led by Sanaka, the divine sages led by Narada,
those liberated while living led by Vamadeva and Shuka, the Yakshas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyadharas and serpents,
Mahashasta, foremost of the Ganas, and the Mothers led by Durga — all the deities that have been named then bowed with joined palms to the supreme Goddess,
standing on auspicious seats and celestial cars. In the middle of the wondrous city created by the mind of the Creator
was the auspicious and most charming temple of the supreme Queen. There, with the glorious Vasudeva, her brother,
the Lord Bhava, Maheshvara, married Gauri before the fire. The drums of the gods sounded and a shower of flowers fell.
Who could describe the auspicious marriage of the divine couple, lords of the worlds, even with a thousand tongues?
In the north-western part of this primal temple of Shri, a vast and excellent abode of the great Lord was fashioned by the Supreme One;
and in the south-eastern part of the house of Shri, a wonderful temple of Vishnu. Thus those three deities are always present there.
Then, having circumambulated, that devoted couple came to the assembly hall, where Brahma and Janardana were.
Coming to the assembled members as prescribed, they joyfully performed the rite with Vedic mantras.
Then before them all, the supreme Goddess, the primal Lakshmi, glanced at Brahma with her right eye and at Hari with her left.
Then there appeared in a mass of light, as if within a cage, the one named Vani and the one named Kamala.
Both, with joined palms, their heads bowed to the Goddess, said, "Victory, Kamakshi, Kamakshi!" and bowed to her.
The Ganga and Yamuna in embodied form came there to serve, and three and a half crores of presiding deities of holy places,
all came to serve Mother Tripura. Then Bharati and Shri, taking chowries in their hands, attended the Goddess, fanning her fittingly.
Seeing those two, Bharati and Shri, born from the eyes of the primal Shri, their creeper-like arms adorned with priceless jewelled bells,
all the people were especially astonished. From then on the auspicious one received the name Kamakshi; by merely uttering it the Goddess grants happiness.
The three syllables "Kamakshi" are the cause of all auspiciousness. Then that Mistress of the world, to the one versed in the Vedas and their limbs,
commanded Sarasvati, "Dwell ever in Brahma." And that mistress of speech, handing her chowrie to the Ganga, entered the Creator's mouth as all the gods watched.
And Indira, instructed likewise by the pleased Mahalakshmi, joyfully went to Vishnu's breast as her fitting dwelling. Bearing her command on their heads, Rama and Vishnu with devotion,
that couple, bowing to Mahatripurasundari, asked again to be her enclosure-deities.
Granting them the boon, "So be it," Tripurasundari made Padma and Achyuta her enclosure-deities.
Placing them to the north of her own seat, he himself stood to the south. Then he said to Mahagauri, "Assume another form." There appeared a charming reflection of Mahagauri,
shining with a divine body, resembling Mahagauri, her two feet with the beauty of the young ruddy sun,
her seat resounding with tinkling bracelets and anklets, with a charming jewelled girdle sounding with flashes like lightning,
her two arms shining with jewelled bracelets and armlets, with an excellent band set with pearls, beryl and rubies,
radiant at the waist, beautiful with three folds, her navel lovely like a whirlpool of the Jahnavi,
her breasts adorned with sandal paste, camphor and saffron, her bodice radiant with pearl ornaments,
a fine chain hanging playfully at her waist, adorned with rings set with pieces of ruby,
charming with a smooth, bright lotus held in her right hand, shining with a garland reaching to her feet and divine ornaments,
the quarters lit by the rays of the gems of her blazing ornaments, adorned with a jewelled necklace set in refined gold,
her neck red with the rays of the jewels of the auspicious thread, adorned with ruby earrings,
her lovely lip-petals with the beauty of hibiscus and coral, resplendent with rows of teeth like pomegranate seeds,
her tender cheeks glowing with a gentle smile, charming with an incomparable, noble nose-gem,
her nose clear and raised with the beauty of a sesame flower, her eyes like blue lotuses sweet in their slight opening,
her brows gracefully arched like a bow of fresh flowers, her forehead like the half-moon and her face lovely as the full moon,
bright with a musk mark of dense fragrance, her lotus face rich with locks like rows of intoxicated bees,
her braid bound with a garland of Parijata flowers, her head adorned with a crown set with priceless jewels —
the abode of all beauty and the home of grace. Shiva and Vishnu, and all the great people there,
then understood the non-difference between that reflection and the Goddess. Then the independent great Goddess entered —
before all the gods as they watched, taking her refuge, she made the reflection and entered it with herself. Seeing her established there, Brahma bowed again and prayed once more:

O perfect Brahman, great Shakti, Mahatripurasundari, renowned as Shri Kamakshi, salutation to you day after day. I make a request today; hear it by your grace.
brahmandpuran:151:98	O Goddess, ever auspicious, let the marriage of Mahagauri and Mahesha be celebrated here every year, for the prosperity of the worlds and for the service of the gods.
brahmandpuran:151:99	O great Goddess, may even the deluded people in this earthly world, seeing her and bowing with devotion, attain the supreme goal.
The supreme one answered him through a voice from the sky, "So be it," and dismissed them all to return to their own abodes.
Remembering again and again that most wondrous conduct, they all bowed to her and went as they had come.
The Grandsire, delighted, together with Mukunda and Shiva, installed her with mantras in that temple of Shri, worshipped her with Vedic hymns, and prostrated himself fully.
Then the Goddess, through a voice from the sky, said this to Brahma:

Having established Vishnu and Shiva in their own places, with a concentrated mind, O firm-willed one, perform service here every year.
brahmandpuran:151:105	Here is the self-manifest Kamagiri seat with the lord of Shri, Mitresha and Amba, standing in the very middle of Shripura,
brahmandpuran:151:106	enclosed on the left side, marked, served by Vishnu elsewhere,
brahmandpuran:151:107	whose form is consciousness and bliss, presiding deity of all seats, of invisible and unmanifest form — he established it according to rule,
brahmandpuran:151:108	in the charming auspicious asterism, with diamond buds of petals, radiant and unassailable, for the prosperity of the worlds.
brahmandpuran:151:109	Now, O Creator, worship it joyfully according to rule, and, having completed the whole mandala, protect your own world.
Thus addressed, the Lord Brahma did as she said, and placing that Goddess in his heart, went to his own abode.
Thus the wondrous conduct of Kamakshi has been truly told to you; know her to be Mahalakshmi herself, O pot-born one.
Whoever hears this daily, or reads it with devotion, holds both enjoyment and liberation in his hand, without doubt.
He becomes equal to Brihaspati in intellect and master of all knowledge. The primal Narayana, the glorious Lord, compassionate to his devotees,
was formerly pleased by my austerity over a long time; the Lord graciously gave my son liberation of sameness of form and taught the greatness of Mahatripurasundari.
Therefore I know something of it from him and shall tell it, not otherwise. I shall tell the secret mantra; hear it attentively.
Neither Brahma nor Vishnu nor Rudra — even these three are deluded by her maya; the fourth is Ishvara. Even Sadashiva does not know her; how then the natural deities?
Sadashiva is the self of all, whose form is being, consciousness and bliss; by her grace he is able to do, to undo and to do otherwise.
Once Maheshvara, thinking "I alone am that," deluded by her maya, helpless, became a corpse.
She alone is the cause of their creation and dissolution. There is a particular point here worth telling; hear it.
Of the three beginning with Brahma, the fourth is the Lord Ishvara; and of all four, Sadashiva is the first creator.
This secret, her wondrous deed, has been told. I shall tell more; listen with attentive mind.
The divine sages led by Narada and the ascetics led by Vasishtha, all of them assembled there, could not then tell the difference between Brahma and the matted-haired Shiva, both being five-faced.
They asked one another, "Who is Brahma and who is Shankara?" While they were talking, Shiva suddenly vanished.
Then between the five-faced Brahma and the white Narayana a dispute arose, each saying, "I am Brahma."
You were born from the lotus of my navel, so you are my son. I am the creator, Brahma, by the likeness of name. You and Rudra are both my sons, sons of the creator.
While those two were thus deluded by maya, Maheshvara appeared between them in the form of a great pillar of light, showing his own greatness to them: "I am Brahman."
Recognising him as the great Lord, Vishnu fell silent. But the five-faced Brahma remained, disregarding him; a circle of light appeared before him above Brahma's heads.
In its midst the god appeared with Uma. Brahma looked up again and, disregarding him, spoke.
Hearing it, the destroyer of Tripura became greatly enraged; Vishnu, seeing this, also became agitated with anger.
From the two of them arose Bhairava, filled with fury; he cut off one of Brahma's heads with his nail. All there cried out "Alas!" and fled.
Then Bhairava shook again and again the skull of Brahma stuck to his nail, yet it did not leave him.
To be freed from that sin of killing a brahmin, he wandered over the earth, to all the holy places and great rivers beginning with the Ganga.

But the skull-bearer was not freed from the sin of brahmin-slaying by them. With a sad face, wretched, he appeared as if bereft of glory. After a long time he reached Kanchi, formerly the dwelling of Brahma.
There, going about for alms daily and serving the supreme Shri, bathing each day at the Panchatirtha marked with auspicious signs,
he stayed for some time, like one bewildered. By dwelling in the holy region of Kanchi, gradually his mind became disciplined;
all his distress shaken off, he meditated on the Goddess, with Lakshmi to serve on the north and Vasudeva on the south.
Coming to Shri Kamakoshtha, he stood before it and, self-controlled, practised meditation on the feet of the primal Lakshmi.
Like a lamp in a windless place, like the ocean without waves, the lord of the mountain did not waver, having restrained the breath within.
Unbroken like a stream of oil, Bhairava without break extended a continuous meditation on the beloved of the mountain's daughter. Neither Brahma nor Vishnu, nor the perfected Kapila,
nor others such as Sanaka, nor sages such as Shuka, were in any way capable of such absorption in samadhi.
Then, through the yoga of contemplating Shri, Shiva attained the state of Shri. The Goddess, pleased, dwelling in a circle of light, stood before him at midnight, and she who is speech spoke:

O Shrikantha, destroyer of all sins, what sin can you have? You are of my form; how can you be embodied? This is only a show for the world.

Bhairava too, delighted and fulfilled by the sight of Shri, spent the rest of that night solely devoted to meditation on the Goddess.
In the morning he bathed at the five great holy places, performed the twilight worship, and again and again shook the skull stuck to his hand.
Yet it did not fall off, and he fell into great despondency: "Is this a dream, or illusion, or merely a confusion of the mind?"
Thinking thus again and again, his mind troubled with grief, Shiva, foremost of the steadfast, then himself restrained his grief.
Bowing to the circle of tulasi and worshipping it, he stood before it and, having restrained all his senses, again entered samadhi.
When a watch had passed, the Goddess came near again: "Enough of samadhi, Shambhu; dive into this lake."
Having instructed him thus, she vanished, and he fell to thinking: "Is this illusion or a dream? What should I do?
'Tomorrow you will be freed from the sin of brahmin-slaying in a moment,' said the supreme Goddess; yet a watch of this day has passed."
Thus, overcome with the thought that everything was false, the Lord heard the voice from the sky thunder, "Dive into the water!"
Hearing it, Shankara gave up his doubt and, resolving on the truth, dived into the lake and rose again in the Ganga.
Seeing Kashi there and wondering what this was, he stood silent for a moment, the skull stuck to his nail.
Seeing the sun burning his forehead, the self-controlled Shiva, bearer of the young moon, entered this city for alms.
Going to some houses and wandering along the street, Bhava saw before him a woman whose form was that of the Goddess.
She gave him alms made of light and quickly vanished; in a moment the skull of Brahma fell from the tip of his nail.
Seeing this wonder, the Lord, his lotus face gladdened, again and again esteemed highly the supreme conduct of Kamakshi.
The city is Kanchi, the holy city; the river is the Kampa, the supreme river; the deity is Kamakshi — such was his reflection.
Thus, freed from distress by the power of the Goddess, Hara, restored to health, went to his own abode, praising the supreme Shri.

The glorious king of Ayodhya named Dasharatha remained without offspring for a long time, afflicted with grief.
The wise king, pure in conduct, summoned in private his family priest Vasishtha, who knew the meaning of all the scriptures, and said:
O revered one, much time has passed and no son has been obtained. My anguish over offspring grows ever greater. What should I do? Tell me, if there is a way to obtain offspring.
Vasishtha said: "O great king of my line, I shall tell you a secret. Ayodhya, Mathura, Maya, Kashi, Kanchi and Avantika — these are declared the holiest, the very best of cities.
By the mere presence of this Mahatripurasundari, the people of Ayodhya worship her as their presiding deity.
There is no other deity equal to her. All others, O king, worship only this Goddess —
Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesha and others with their consorts, always and forever. With rows of coconuts, jackfruits and plantains,
with abundant honey, ghee and sugar, with heaps of sweet milk-rice and special prepared offerings, one should worship Tripurambika; she herself will soon grant us our wish."
Having honoured the teacher who spoke thus with pleasing gifts, the lord of the people dismissed him, eager to obtain a son of his own.
Then, in the very way the teacher had told, the king of kings worshipped Lalita, the supreme Queen, with supreme devotion.
Thus performing worship every day with a pleased mind, he lay down there in the abode of the deity of Ayodhya.
When midnight had passed and the lamp glowed quietly, as he was slightly drowsy, Tripurambika,
her four arms adorned with noose, goad, bow and arrows, rich in amorous attire and adorned with every ornament, stood before the son of Indumati and softly spoke these words:

O glorious, sinless Dasharatha, you are destined to have sons; but there are acts of betrayal of trust committed by you in former times.
